title: Your Brain Runs on Shortcuts (And They Betray You)
subtitle: Evolution built you a fast, lazy autopilot that's brilliant most of the time and predictably, hilariously wrong the rest.
hook: Quick: a bat and ball cost $1.10 together, the bat costs $1 more than the ball — how much is the ball? If '10 cents' popped into your head, congrats: your brain just took a shortcut, and it's wrong (it's 5 cents). You have two thinking modes — a fast, effortless autopilot and a slow, deliberate analyst — and the autopilot runs the show. Today: the predictable ways it fools you, and how to catch it.

builds_on.label: The Math of Every Good Bet

sections.heading: System 1 and System 2
sections.body: Psychologist Daniel Kahneman split thinking into two modes. **System 1** is fast, automatic, emotional — it recognizes faces, dodges balls, and jumps to the '10 cents' answer. **System 2** is slow, effortful, logical — the one that actually does the subtraction. System 1 handles ~99% of life brilliantly. The trouble: it also fires confidently on problems that *need* System 2, and you don't notice the handoff never happened.

sections.caption: System 1 answers first — fast and confident. Only if you deliberately engage System 2 does the careful answer get a chance.

sections.label: A few biases to know by name
sections.body: Anchoring — the first number you hear drags your estimate toward it. Availability — vivid, recent examples feel more common than they are (plane crashes vs. car crashes). Confirmation bias — you notice evidence that fits your belief and skip the rest. Loss aversion — losing $100 hurts about twice as much as gaining $100 feels good. Naming them is half the defense.

sections.label: You can't turn them off
sections.body: Knowing about biases doesn't disable them — System 1 still fires. What works is building *habits and systems*: sleep on big decisions, write down predictions, ask 'what would change my mind?', and get an outside view. You don't out-think biases; you design around them.

sections.caption: An animated guide to Kahneman's two systems and how they shape every decision.

takeaways: Thinking has two modes: **System 1** (fast, automatic) and **System 2** (slow, effortful).
System 1 runs most of life well — but fires confidently on problems that need System 2.
Know the big biases: **anchoring, availability, confirmation bias, loss aversion**.
Awareness alone doesn't disable a bias — the reflex still fires.
Beat them with **systems**: slow down, write predictions, seek outside views.

quiz.explain: System 1 is the gut-fast autopilot; System 2 is the slow analyst.

quiz.q: You judge plane travel as more dangerous than driving because crashes are vivid in the news. Which bias?
quiz.explain: Availability: easily-recalled, vivid examples feel more frequent than they are.

quiz.q: CALLBACK + BOSS: Bayes (Day 3) told you to weigh the base rate. Which bias is basically 'ignoring the base rate because a story feels compelling'?
options: The representativeness/availability trap — vivid stories override dull base rates
quiz.explain: A gripping narrative makes System 1 forget how rare the thing actually is — the exact failure Bayes fixes. Biases and probability are two views of the same weakness.

tg_quiz.q: Bat + ball = $1.10; bat is $1 more than the ball. The ball costs…
tg_quiz.correct: Nice — you engaged System 2. It's 5 cents.
tg_quiz.explain: The gut answer feels right and is wrong — that's the whole lesson.
